items.title: Free and properly discontinuous group actions
items.statement: A group action on a topological space is free when no nonidentity element fixes a point and properly discontinuous when for every compact subset only finitely many group elements move it to meet it; the equivalent finitely-many-translates consequence used on surfaces is recorded.

references.title: Donald E. Marshall, The Uniformization Theorem
references.locator: PDF pp. 1-15, especially Lemmas 1-5, Theorem 4, Corollary 6, and the non-Green proof

references.title: Mikhail Lyubich, Dynamics of Quadratic Polynomials, Vol. I
references.locator: Ch. 1 §§2.4 and 5, printed pp. 64-68 and 115-118, Theorems 5.1-5.6

references.title: Curtis T. McMullen, Riemann Surfaces, Math 213b course notes
references.locator: Ch. 16 printed pp. 146-147 for hyperbolic geometry; Ch. 17 printed p. 157 for uniformization statement only

items.title: A universal covering of a Riemann surface inherits a unique holomorphic atlas
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. The topological universal cover of a connected Riemann surface is a second-countable Riemann surface with the unique complex structure making the projection a holomorphic unbranched covering; every deck transformation is biholomorphic.

references.title: Donald E. Marshall, The Uniformization Theorem
references.locator: PDF pp. 1-15, especially Lemmas 1-5, Theorem 4, Corollary 6, and the non-Green proof

references.title: Mikhail Lyubich, Dynamics of Quadratic Polynomials, Vol. I
references.locator: Ch. 1 §§2.4 and 5, printed pp. 64-68 and 115-118, Theorems 5.1-5.6

items.proof_strategy: Use a countable basis of relatively compact coordinate discs. Their overlap components are countable; under Countable Choice choose a path in each, and subdivide any compact loop into finitely many such discs to represent its homotopy class by a finite word. Thus the fundamental group and each universal-cover fibre are countable. Lifts of countably many evenly covered base discs then form a countable basis upstairs. Pull back each base chart through each covering sheet; overlap transitions are the original holomorphic chart transitions. This atlas is unique because the projection is locally biholomorphic. A deck map is locally the composition of two inverse sheets, so it and its inverse are holomorphic.

items.title: Plane subharmonicity is invariant under biholomorphic change of coordinate
items.statement: Let $G:\Omega_1\to\Omega_2$ be a biholomorphism of complex domains. A function $u:\Omega_2\to[-\infty,\infty)$ is subharmonic on $\Omega_2$ if and only if $u\circ G$ is subharmonic on $\Omega_1$.

references.title: Harold P. Boas, Class Notes Math 618: Complex Variables II, Spring 2016, §7.2 (standard ways to produce subharmonic functions: u∘f for u subharmonic and f holomorphic)

items.proof_strategy: Biholomorphic pullback preserves upper semicontinuity and the failure of being identically -infinity on components. For the harmonic-comparison form of subharmonicity, conjugate a candidate majorant h on a disc by the inverse biholomorphism; the resulting plane harmonic function H has the same boundary domination, and the maximum principle applied to u∘G-H forces the comparison to hold inside. Apply the implication in both directions using G and G^{-1}.

items.title: Chartwise harmonic and subharmonic functions on a Riemann surface
items.statement: Real-valued harmonic and extended-real-valued subharmonic functions on a Riemann surface are defined chartwise; the Laplacian expressions depend on the chart, their vanishing does not, and harmonic conjugates use u+iv.

references.title: Donald E. Marshall, The Uniformization Theorem
references.locator: PDF pp. 1-15, especially Lemmas 1-5, Theorem 4, Corollary 6, and the non-Green proof

references.title: Mikhail Lyubich, Dynamics of Quadratic Polynomials, Vol. I
references.locator: Ch. 1 §§2.4 and 5, printed pp. 64-68 and 115-118, Theorems 5.1-5.6

items.strategy: Conformal changes multiply the plane Laplacian by the positive factor |f′| squared, and preserve the submean comparison definition; hence the chartwise notions agree on overlaps. Fix Δ=∂x squared+∂y squared and the positive Green pole -log|z|. The Hodge-star convention is *dx=dy, *dy=-dx, so dv=*du is the Cauchy-Riemann system.

items.title: Locality of subharmonicity in the plane and on Riemann surfaces
items.statement: Plane domains: an upper semicontinuous function on a complex domain that is subharmonic on a connected open neighbourhood of each of its points is subharmonic. Riemann surfaces: an upper semicontinuous function on an open subset of a Riemann surface that is subharmonic on an open neighbourhood of each of its points is subharmonic. No choice principle is used.

references.title: Donald E. Marshall, The Uniformization Theorem
references.locator: PDF p. 1 (plane theorems depending only on local behaviour hold on Riemann surfaces) and PDF pp. 1-2 (chartwise definition of harmonic and subharmonic functions on a surface)

items.proof_strategy: Reduce the plane statement to the harmonic-majorant characterisation: on a closed disc the difference u-h is upper semicontinuous, so its finite maximum over the compact disc is attained; the harmonic-comparison obligation follows from the maximum principle on the open disc, whose maximum set is clopen in a connected neighbourhood on which u is subharmonic. The surface statement is chartwise, using that subharmonicity on a surface is defined chartwise and invariant under biholomorphic change of coordinate.

items.title: Harmonic conjugates and integral logarithmic-pole monodromy on surfaces
items.statement: On a simply connected Riemann surface every real harmonic function has a global harmonic conjugate. On such a surface, if u is harmonic away from finitely many points and u=-m_j log|z_j|+h_j near each one with integer m_j and harmonic h_j, exponentiating the negative of its locally holomorphic complexification gives a single-valued meromorphic function whose order at that point is m_j and which has no other zeros or poles.

references.title: Donald E. Marshall, The Uniformization Theorem
references.locator: PDF pp. 1-15, especially Lemmas 1-5, Theorem 4, Corollary 6, and the non-Green proof

references.title: Mikhail Lyubich, Dynamics of Quadratic Polynomials, Vol. I
references.locator: Ch. 1 §§2.4 and 5, printed pp. 64-68 and 115-118, Theorems 5.1-5.6

items.proof_strategy: Locally integrate *du to a conjugate v. The form *du is closed because Delta u=0; subdivide homotopies into finitely many chart rectangles and cancel their boundary integrals, proving homotopy invariance of path integrals on an abstract surface. On a simply connected surface all periods vanish when u has no poles. With a pole u=-m log|z|+h, the conjugate period around it is -2pi m; all periods on the punctured simply connected surface are integral multiples of 2pi because its first homology is generated by the puncture loops. Thus exp(-(u+iv)) is single valued, and near the pole it is z^m times a nonvanishing holomorphic factor. Positive m gives a zero, negative m a pole; away from the listed points its modulus is exp(-u)>0. No plane-domain monodromy theorem is applied directly to the abstract surface.

items.title: Regular exhaustion and Dirichlet solutions on relatively compact surface domains
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. A noncompact Riemann surface has an exhaustion by connected relatively compact smooth bordered domains. Every such domain with smooth boundary has a unique harmonic extension of each continuous boundary datum.

references.title: Donald E. Marshall, The Uniformization Theorem
references.locator: PDF pp. 1-15, especially Lemmas 1-5, Theorem 4, Corollary 6, and the non-Green proof

references.title: Mikhail Lyubich, Dynamics of Quadratic Polynomials, Vol. I
references.locator: Ch. 1 §§2.4 and 5, printed pp. 64-68 and 115-118, Theorems 5.1-5.6

items.proof_strategy: A holomorphic atlas is a smooth atlas. Apply the published proper smooth exhaustion and Morse-Sard to choose increasing regular levels; take the component containing a fixed compact core and fill bounded complementary components, retaining smooth finite boundary. For continuous boundary data, use the chartwise Perron lower family, finite maxima and local Poisson replacement. Harnack control proves its finite envelope harmonic on each chart. A smooth boundary is locally one-sided and admits an explicit exterior-circle or linear-coordinate barrier, so the Perron envelope takes the prescribed limit at each boundary point. Maximum principle gives uniqueness. Each passage is local except the countable exhaustion; Countable Choice is used through the cited exhaustion and Sard suppliers.

items.title: Canonical Green kernel on a Riemann surface
items.statement: For a surface X and pole p, take the Perron envelope of nonnegative compactly supported subharmonic functions on X minus p having at most a unit logarithmic pole at p. When finite, this defines the canonical positive Green kernel g_X(.,p), with g_X+log|z| harmonic near p.

references.title: Donald E. Marshall, The Uniformization Theorem
references.locator: PDF pp. 1-15, especially Lemmas 1-5, Theorem 4, Corollary 6, and the non-Green proof

references.title: Mikhail Lyubich, Dynamics of Quadratic Polynomials, Vol. I
references.locator: Ch. 1 §§2.4 and 5, printed pp. 64-68 and 115-118, Theorems 5.1-5.6

items.strategy: Fix a local coordinate z(p)=0. Candidates vanish outside a compact subset of X and satisfy limsup(v+log|z|)<infinity near p. Changing z adds a bounded harmonic logarithm, so the condition is coordinate independent. Define the envelope; its harmonicity, positivity, pole normalization and leastness are proved in the next lemma. Do not identify this kernel with the earlier plane-domain Green definition without checking conventions.

items.title: Green envelope dichotomy, pole and leastness on a Riemann surface
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. For the canonical surface Green family, the envelope is either infinite everywhere off the pole or a positive harmonic function there whose sum with log|z| extends harmonically across the pole. In the finite case it is the least positive harmonic function with that unit pole.

references.title: Donald E. Marshall, The Uniformization Theorem
references.locator: PDF pp. 1-15, especially Lemmas 1-5, Theorem 4, Corollary 6, and the non-Green proof

references.title: Mikhail Lyubich, Dynamics of Quadratic Polynomials, Vol. I
references.locator: Ch. 1 §§2.4 and 5, printed pp. 64-68 and 115-118, Theorems 5.1-5.6

references.title: Charles Favre, Riemann surfaces
references.locator: Section 2.3.3: Def. 2.3.3 (Perron families: max-stability and stability under Poisson modification), Lemma 2.3.11, and Prop. 2.3.12 with its proof (increasing harmonic balayage, Harnack, and the maximum-principle comparison identifying the supremum)

items.proof_strategy: The compactly supported function -log|z| on a unit chart disc, zero outside, makes the Perron family nonempty. Finite maxima and Poisson replacement stay in the family. At a point, choose an increasing sequence approaching the supremum; Harnack chains give the all-infinite or locally uniform harmonic alternative, and comparison of two such sequences identifies the envelope everywhere. Near the pole compare with local -log|z| below and use the maximum principle on a coordinate circle above; bounded harmonic correction extends across the puncture. For any competing positive harmonic unit-pole function H, v-(1+epsilon)H is subharmonic at the pole and nonpositive off the compact support of v, hence v<=H on letting epsilon tend to zero. Take the supremum. Countable Choice licenses the sequences.

items.title: Removing a compact chart disc gives a Greenian surface
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. If U is a relatively compact coordinate disc in a connected Riemann surface X and X minus its closure is nonempty, the connected exterior X minus closure(U) has a finite canonical Green kernel at every pole in that exterior.

references.title: Donald E. Marshall, The Uniformization Theorem
references.locator: PDF pp. 1-15, especially Lemmas 1-5, Theorem 4, Corollary 6, and the non-Green proof

references.title: Mikhail Lyubich, Dynamics of Quadratic Polynomials, Vol. I
references.locator: Ch. 1 §§2.4 and 5, printed pp. 64-68 and 115-118, Theorems 5.1-5.6

items.proof_strategy: Detour paths around the embedded closed disc to show the exterior is connected. Fix another small disc about the pole. Solve the surface Dirichlet problem on the complement of that pole disc in the exterior, with value one at its inner circle and zero at the removed chart circle; exhaustion and Perron comparison give a harmonic barrier omega strictly between zero and one. Any compact-support Green competitor v satisfies max on the outer pole circle <= c max on the inner pole circle, where c<1 is the maximum of omega there. Comparing v+log|z| in the pole annulus supplies the complementary logarithmic bound, so the inner maximum is uniformly bounded. The Green envelope is finite and the preceding dichotomy gives the kernel. Treat boundary circles as deleted from the open exterior, not as points of a Riemann surface.

items.title: Green second identity on a smooth bordered Riemann-surface domain
items.statement: Let Omega be a relatively compact smooth bordered domain of a Riemann surface. For real functions u,v that are C² up to its smooth boundary away from finitely many logarithmic poles, the conformally invariant Green second identity holds on Omega with small coordinate circles deleted. In particular, when u and v are harmonic off those poles and vanish on the outer boundary, the total inner-circle flux vanishes.

references.title: Donald E. Marshall, The Uniformization Theorem
references.locator: PDF p.15, Comment 5: Green-theorem route to Green-kernel symmetry; the scaffold supplies the chartwise finite-cell proof.

items.proof_strategy: Remove finitely many disjoint coordinate discs about the poles. Cover the remaining compact smooth bordered domain by finitely many holomorphic coordinate charts and subdivide it into finitely many chart-contained piecewise smooth cells, matching edge subdivisions on both sides. In each chart integrate div(u grad v-v grad u)=u Delta v-v Delta u by the elementary planar Green formula (first prove it on graph-bounded rectangles by Fubini, then add finitely many cells). On overlaps a holomorphic change of chart multiplies the Laplacian and area density by reciprocal factors, while the outward conormal line integral is unchanged; hence the identity is intrinsic. Interior edge integrals cancel in opposite orientations. When u,v are harmonic off the removed discs, the area integral is zero; the remaining boundary terms are the outer boundary and the small circles. Smoothness of the outer boundary gives the usual conormal there, and if u=v=0 on that boundary its contribution vanishes. This finite-cell argument is choice free and proves the needed special surface Green identity directly, without importing the out-of-plan general Stokes page.

items.title: Symmetry of the canonical surface Green kernel
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. If a Riemann surface has finite canonical Green kernels at two distinct poles p and q, then g_X(p,q)=g_X(q,p). On an exhaustion by smooth bordered domains, the finite-domain zero-boundary kernels increase to the canonical kernel.

references.title: Donald E. Marshall, The Uniformization Theorem
references.locator: PDF pp. 1-15, especially Lemmas 1-5, Theorem 4, Corollary 6, and the non-Green proof

references.title: Mikhail Lyubich, Dynamics of Quadratic Polynomials, Vol. I
references.locator: Ch. 1 §§2.4 and 5, printed pp. 64-68 and 115-118, Theorems 5.1-5.6

items.proof_strategy: Construct the zero-boundary kernel on each smooth exhaustion domain by Perron with a local -log|z| pole. It is positive; domain comparison makes the sequence increasing, and the global kernel bounds it. Harnack convergence gives a harmonic limit. The local log correction remains bounded above and below near the pole and extends; comparison against each positive global candidate proves that the limit is precisely the canonical kernel. For two poles on one exhaustion domain, apply the preceding chartwise Green identity outside small coordinate circles. On the outer boundary u=v=0, while the two inner circles contribute opposite 2pi times the two cross values; shrink the circles to obtain equality. Take limits. The local Green identity supplies the required boundary integration and no general Stokes result is consumed.

items.title: Locally bounded harmonic families have harmonic subsequential limits
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. A locally uniformly bounded sequence of real harmonic functions on a Riemann surface admits a subsequence converging locally uniformly to a harmonic function; distributional limits in charts are smooth by Weyl’s lemma.

references.title: Donald E. Marshall, The Uniformization Theorem
references.locator: PDF pp. 1-15, especially Lemmas 1-5, Theorem 4, Corollary 6, and the non-Green proof

references.title: Mikhail Lyubich, Dynamics of Quadratic Polynomials, Vol. I
references.locator: Ch. 1 §§2.4 and 5, printed pp. 64-68 and 115-118, Theorems 5.1-5.6

items.proof_strategy: Differentiate the Poisson kernel on concentric chart discs to get interior gradient bounds from local sup bounds, hence equicontinuity. Use a countable chart compact exhaustion and diagonal Arzela-Ascoli selection under Countable Choice. Locally uniform convergence implies distributional convergence; integrating by parts gives ΔT=0 on each chart. Weyl’s lemma identifies the limit with a smooth harmonic representative; continuity makes that representative the pointwise limit. Check compatibility on overlaps. This is the exact Weyl and normal-family passage used for the dipole limit.

items.title: A simply connected Greenian Riemann surface is a disc
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. A simply connected Riemann surface with a finite canonical Green kernel is biholomorphic to the unit disc.

references.title: Donald E. Marshall, The Uniformization Theorem
references.locator: PDF pp. 1-15, especially Lemmas 1-5, Theorem 4, Corollary 6, and the non-Green proof

references.title: Mikhail Lyubich, Dynamics of Quadratic Polynomials, Vol. I
references.locator: Ch. 1 §§2.4 and 5, printed pp. 64-68 and 115-118, Theorems 5.1-5.6

items.proof_strategy: At p, take the global harmonic conjugate of g_p on X minus p, correct its -2pi pole period, and exponentiate to a holomorphic f_p:X->D with a simple zero at p and |f_p|=exp(-g_p). At q compose f_p with a disc automorphism sending f_p(q) to zero. Leastness bounds g_q above by minus its log modulus. At p, symmetry of Green kernels makes this inequality an equality. On the complement of q and the other zeros of the transformed map, the nonnegative difference is harmonic and attains its minimum zero at p. This complement is connected because a discrete subset does not disconnect a surface; the strong maximum principle makes the difference zero throughout, and extension across the deleted zeros shows there were no other zeros and the zero at q was simple. Thus f_p is injective. Its image is a simply connected proper plane domain, so the published Riemann mapping theorem gives a biholomorphism of the image with D. Full AC enters through that theorem; the surface Green and symmetry suppliers require only Countable Choice.

items.title: A dipole Green function exists on a Riemann surface
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. For distinct p and q on a connected Riemann surface X there is a real function G harmonic off p and q, bounded off disjoint coordinate discs around them, with G+log|z_p| and G-log|z_q| extending harmonically at p and q.

references.title: Donald E. Marshall, The Uniformization Theorem
references.locator: PDF pp. 1-15, especially Lemmas 1-5, Theorem 4, Corollary 6, and the non-Green proof

references.title: Mikhail Lyubich, Dynamics of Quadratic Polynomials, Vol. I
references.locator: Ch. 1 §§2.4 and 5, printed pp. 64-68 and 115-118, Theorems 5.1-5.6

items.proof_strategy: Choose a third point a away from p and q and shrink a coordinate disc U_t about a. On X minus closure(U_t), the puncture lemma supplies kernels g_t(.,p), g_t(.,q). For a fixed smaller pole disc about p, let M_p(t) be the maximum of g_t(.,p) on its inner boundary. The maximum principle bounds g_t(.,p) by M_p(t) off that disc; the logarithmic comparison across its annulus bounds M_p(t) minus the Green value at some point on the outer circle independently of t. Hence the positive harmonic function M_p(t)-g_t(.,p) is bounded on each fixed compact away from p by Harnack chains, uniformly in t. Repeat at q. Symmetry gives g_t(q,p)=g_t(p,q), so the two unknown additive constants cancel in G_t=g_t(.,p)-g_t(.,q); it is uniformly bounded on fixed circles around p and q and on fixed compact sets away from them. The maximum principle propagates this to a uniform bound on the whole exterior of fixed pole discs. Apply local harmonic compactness and a countable diagonal subsequence as t tends to zero. Limits of the pole-corrected functions are harmonic on the pole discs by the uniform boundary bounds; the bounded puncture at a is removable. The resulting G has exactly opposite unit logarithmic poles and remains bounded off the discs. No Green kernel on all of X is assumed.

items.title: A simply connected surface without a Green kernel is plane or sphere
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. A simply connected Riemann surface whose canonical Green envelope is infinite is biholomorphic to the complex plane if noncompact, and to the Riemann sphere if compact.

references.title: Donald E. Marshall, The Uniformization Theorem
references.locator: PDF pp. 1-15, especially Lemmas 1-5, Theorem 4, Corollary 6, and the non-Green proof

references.title: Mikhail Lyubich, Dynamics of Quadratic Polynomials, Vol. I
references.locator: Ch. 1 §§2.4 and 5, printed pp. 64-68 and 115-118, Theorems 5.1-5.6

items.proof_strategy: First, a nonconstant bounded holomorphic h would give a finite upper bound on each compact-support Green competitor v by applying the maximum principle to v+(1+epsilon)log|B(h)|, where B sends h(p) to zero; the Green dichotomy forbids it. Exponentiate the dipole complexification, using the +1 and -1 integral periods, to obtain a meromorphic map F:X->sphere with one simple zero p and one simple pole q. For any r use the dipole with zero r and pole q to get F_r; the quotient (F-F(r))/F_r is holomorphic and bounded outside the pole discs, hence globally bounded and therefore constant on a nonGreen surface. It is nonzero by evaluating at p or q, so F takes the value F(r) only at r. Thus F is injective. If its simply connected image omitted two sphere points, a Möbius change would put it in a proper simply connected plane domain and the Riemann mapping theorem would yield a nonconstant bounded holomorphic function, contradiction. Hence the image omits at most one point; compactness distinguishes sphere from plane. Full AC is inherited from Riemann mapping.

items.title: The sphere, plane and disc are pairwise biholomorphically distinct
items.statement: The Riemann sphere, complex plane and unit disc are simply connected Riemann surfaces; no two are biholomorphic.

references.title: Donald E. Marshall, The Uniformization Theorem
references.locator: PDF pp. 1-15, especially Lemmas 1-5, Theorem 4, Corollary 6, and the non-Green proof

references.title: Mikhail Lyubich, Dynamics of Quadratic Polynomials, Vol. I
references.locator: Ch. 1 §§2.4 and 5, printed pp. 64-68 and 115-118, Theorems 5.1-5.6

items.proof_strategy: The sphere is compact while the plane and disc are noncompact. A biholomorphism C->D would be a nonconstant bounded entire function, contrary to Liouville. Simple connectivity of sphere, plane and disc follows from their standard topological contractions or sphere loop theorem; no choice is used.

items.title: Uniformization of simply connected Riemann surfaces
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Every simply connected Riemann surface is biholomorphic to exactly one of the Riemann sphere, complex plane and unit disc.

references.title: Donald E. Marshall, The Uniformization Theorem
references.locator: PDF pp. 1-15, especially Lemmas 1-5, Theorem 4, Corollary 6, and the non-Green proof

references.title: Mikhail Lyubich, Dynamics of Quadratic Polynomials, Vol. I
references.locator: Ch. 1 §§2.4 and 5, printed pp. 64-68 and 115-118, Theorems 5.1-5.6

items.proof_strategy: Fix p and form the canonical surface Green envelope. Its dichotomy is finite or infinite. In the finite case the Green-function branch supplies a biholomorphism to D. In the infinite case the dipole branch supplies a biholomorphism to C or the sphere according to compactness. The model inequivalence lemma gives uniqueness. Both branches use abstract-surface Green/Dirichlet arguments; the earlier plane-domain mapping theorem is invoked only after the new Green map embeds the surface into C. AC enters through the two branch lemmas’ calls to the published Riemann mapping theorem, while countable choices enter the exhaustion and normal-family construction.

items.title: Spherical, parabolic and hyperbolic universal-covering types
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. A connected Riemann surface is spherical, parabolic or hyperbolic according as its holomorphic universal cover is biholomorphic to the sphere, plane or disc; exactly one type occurs.

references.title: Donald E. Marshall, The Uniformization Theorem
references.locator: PDF pp. 1-15, especially Lemmas 1-5, Theorem 4, Corollary 6, and the non-Green proof

references.title: Mikhail Lyubich, Dynamics of Quadratic Polynomials, Vol. I
references.locator: Ch. 1 §§2.4 and 5, printed pp. 64-68 and 115-118, Theorems 5.1-5.6

items.strategy: Existence and the lifted complex structure come from the covering lemma; uniqueness of universal covers over X is holomorphic because the projection determines local charts. Uniformization and pairwise model inequivalence make exactly one label possible. This is a universal-cover classification, not the potential-theoretic Greenian/parabolic terminology: a hyperbolic universal cover need not imply X itself has a Green function (for example C minus two points). The definition inherits full AC only through uniformization.

items.title: Every Riemann surface is a quotient of a simply connected model
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Every connected Riemann surface is biholomorphic to the quotient of exactly one of the sphere, plane or disc by a group of holomorphic automorphisms acting freely and properly discontinuously.

references.title: Donald E. Marshall, The Uniformization Theorem
references.locator: PDF pp. 1-15, especially Lemmas 1-5, Theorem 4, Corollary 6, and the non-Green proof

references.title: Mikhail Lyubich, Dynamics of Quadratic Polynomials, Vol. I
references.locator: Ch. 1 §§2.4 and 5, printed pp. 64-68 and 115-118, Theorems 5.1-5.6

items.proof_strategy: Uniformize the holomorphic universal cover and conjugate its deck group into the automorphism group of the chosen model. The deck action is free by the published proposition; evenly covered neighborhoods give small sheets with no nonidentity translates meeting them and thus proper discontinuity. The universal-cover deck group acts transitively on each fibre by the published deck/fundamental-group theorem, so the orbit quotient is precisely X, and the local quotient charts agree holomorphically with its atlas. Exactly one model type follows from the preceding definition. No claim that the deck group itself is unique up to equality is made.

items.title: Poincaré metric on a hyperbolic Riemann surface
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. On a surface with disc universal cover, the Poincaré length element is the local pushforward of 2|dz|/(1-|z|²) along the holomorphic universal covering; it is independent of local inverse and of the uniformization.

references.title: Donald E. Marshall, The Uniformization Theorem
references.locator: PDF pp. 1-15, especially Lemmas 1-5, Theorem 4, Corollary 6, and the non-Green proof

references.title: Mikhail Lyubich, Dynamics of Quadratic Polynomials, Vol. I
references.locator: Ch. 1 §§2.4 and 5, printed pp. 64-68 and 115-118, Theorems 5.1-5.6

items.strategy: For a covering p:D->X and an evenly covered chart V, let s:V->D be any inverse sheet and set rho_X(w)|dw|=2|s′(w)|/(1-|s(w)|²)|dw|. Two inverse sheets differ on a connected overlap by a deck transformation, which is a disc automorphism; the published disc-automorphism invariance preserves this tensor. A different uniformization differs by a disc automorphism as well. Thus the positive smooth metric patches globally, with curvature -1 inherited locally from the disc. The construction itself makes no new choice once the cover is supplied; AC is inherited through the type definition.

items.title: Deck transformations preserve the hyperbolic metric
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. For a disc uniformization of a hyperbolic Riemann surface, every deck transformation preserves the Poincaré metric and distance; the quotient metric is precisely the surface Poincaré metric.

references.title: Donald E. Marshall, The Uniformization Theorem
references.locator: PDF pp. 1-15, especially Lemmas 1-5, Theorem 4, Corollary 6, and the non-Green proof

references.title: Mikhail Lyubich, Dynamics of Quadratic Polynomials, Vol. I
references.locator: Ch. 1 §§2.4 and 5, printed pp. 64-68 and 115-118, Theorems 5.1-5.6

items.proof_strategy: A deck transformation is biholomorphic by the covering-structure lemma, hence a disc automorphism. Use the published disc metric identity 2|dγ(z)|/(1-|γ(z)|²)=2|dz|/(1-|z|²); integrate along curves to obtain distance invariance. The definition of the surface tensor is the unique local tensor whose pullback by the covering is the disc tensor, so it descends. AC is inherited through the surface metric definition; a fixed cover needs no new choice.

items.title: A compact free affine plane quotient comes from a rank-two lattice
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. If a group G of biholomorphisms of the complex plane acts freely and properly discontinuously and C/G is compact, then every nonidentity element is a translation, G is a rank-two lattice of translations, and C/G is a complex torus of genus one.

references.title: Curtis T. McMullen, Riemann Surfaces, Math 213b course notes
references.locator: Ch. 2, Theorem 2.6, printed p. 7: classification of plane quotients as C, C*, or C/Lambda; lattice case for compact quotients.

references.title: Mikhail Lyubich, Dynamics of Quadratic Polynomials, Vol. I
references.locator: Ch. 1 §5, Theorems 5.1–5.2, printed pp. 115–116: quotient classification by universal-cover type.

items.proof_strategy: Every plane automorphism is az+b. If a!=1 it fixes b/(1-a), contradicting freeness, so G is a discrete additive subgroup of C. Discreteness follows from proper discontinuity on a compact disc. Project G to a line perpendicular to a shortest nonzero vector v; if the projection accumulated at 0, reduce representatives modulo Zv into a bounded strip, obtaining an accumulation in G, contradiction. Thus the projection is either 0 or hZ. Compactness of C/G rules out projection 0 and gives a nonzero h. Choose w with projection h; subtract multiples of w and then v to show G=Zv+Zw, with v,w real-linearly independent. The closed fundamental parallelogram is compact and its opposite-edge identifications form the one-handle torus; by the published topological genus definition the quotient has genus one. Full AC is inherited through that genus definition, not needed for the finite lattice argument.

items.title: Compact genus determines universal-covering type
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. A compact Riemann surface of genus 0 has spherical type, genus 1 has parabolic type, and genus at least 2 has hyperbolic type.

references.title: Donald E. Marshall, The Uniformization Theorem
references.locator: PDF pp. 1-15, especially Lemmas 1-5, Theorem 4, Corollary 6, and the non-Green proof

references.title: Mikhail Lyubich, Dynamics of Quadratic Polynomials, Vol. I
references.locator: Ch. 1 §§2.4 and 5, printed pp. 64-68 and 115-118, Theorems 5.1-5.6

items.proof_strategy: Write a compact surface X as U/G by universal-cover classification. If U is the sphere, every nonidentity Möbius map has a fixed point, contradicting the free deck action; G is trivial, so X is the genus-zero sphere. If U=C, the preceding lattice lemma makes X a complex torus of genus one. If U=D, compactness makes G nontrivial. A nonidentity deck automorphism is fixed-point-free in D, hence in its Möbius normal form is hyperbolic (two boundary fixed points) or parabolic (one). To exclude genus zero, its topological sphere has trivial fundamental group, so the universal-cover deck group would be trivial. To exclude genus one, the topological classification identifies X with the square torus; the explicit translation cover C->C/(Z+iZ) computes its fundamental group as Z² by the published universal-cover/deck theorem. Thus G would be abelian and noncyclic. But a commuting disc automorphism preserves the boundary fixed set of a nonidentity element. For a hyperbolic element, swapping its two fixed points conjugates it to its inverse and cannot commute; after conjugating fixed points to 0 and infinity in the half-plane, all commuting elements are positive real scalings z->az. For a parabolic element, conjugate its fixed point to infinity and it to z->z+1; commuting elements are real translations z->z+t. In either case a discrete subgroup of this one-parameter real group is cyclic: discreteness follows from proper discontinuity, and the elementary least-positive-element argument applies. This contradicts G=Z². Hence a compact disc quotient has genus at least two. The three cases exhaust all compact surfaces, proving both directions. AC is inherited through genus and uniformization, not introduced by the finite group calculation.

title: Hyperbolic Riemann Surfaces and Uniformization: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: Hyperbolic distances and geodesics in disc and half-plane
items.statement: Under the Cayley map the disc metric 2|dz|/(1-|z|²) becomes |dw|/Im(w); radial disc segments and vertical half-plane rays give d_D(0,r)=2 artanh(r) and d_H(i,iy)=|log y|, and geodesics are orthogonal circles or lines.

items.proof_strategy: Differentiate the Cayley map and substitute in the metric. Integrate along the radial and vertical curves, compare with the published distance formula to prove minimality, then move these curves by disc/half-plane automorphisms. Their images are Euclidean circles or lines meeting the boundary orthogonally.

items.title: Annulus and punctured disc have hyperbolic universal covers
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. The exponential maps a vertical strip onto a finite annulus and a left half-plane onto the punctured disc; both covering domains are biholomorphic to the disc, and their deck groups are generated by translation by 2pi i.

items.proof_strategy: For 0<r<1 use {log r<Re w<0} and exp(w), checking the exact 2pi i deck shifts and even covering over every point. Map the strip explicitly to a half-plane by an exponential of a scaled rotated coordinate and then by Cayley to D. For D* use {Re w<0} and exp(w), followed by Cayley. The two surfaces are therefore hyperbolic in the universal-cover sense even though their conformal moduli differ. AC is inherited through the type and quotient theorems.

items.title: A complex torus has a lattice of parabolic deck translations
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. For a rank-two lattice Lambda in C, the universal covering C->C/Lambda has deck group {z->z+lambda:lambda in Lambda}; the compact quotient has genus 1 and parabolic universal-covering type.

items.proof_strategy: For Lambda=Z omega_1+Z omega_2 with Im(omega_2/omega_1)>0, lattice discreteness gives a small disc disjoint from all nonzero translates, so its translates yield evenly covered holomorphic quotient charts on C/Lambda. C is simply connected. Every deck map is determined by the image of 0 and hence is translation by some lambda in Lambda; all such translations are deck maps. A closed fundamental parallelogram covers the quotient, so it is compact; the opposite-edge identifications are the standard one-handle torus, hence genus one by the published genus definition. Its universal cover is C and the type is parabolic. This construction repeats the needed chart and genus calculation inline and uses no earlier B-page example.

items.title: A genus-two compact surface gives a cocompact Fuchsian group
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. For six distinct complex numbers a_1,...,a_6, the compact hyperelliptic Riemann surface obtained by completing y²=prod(x-a_j) has genus two and a disc universal cover. Its deck group is a torsion-free discrete subgroup of Aut(D), and the surface is a cocompact Fuchsian quotient.

items.proof_strategy: Construct X directly from y²=P(x) with six distinct roots. The holomorphic implicit-function theorem gives charts on the smooth affine curve; at a_j use y as local coordinate and x-a_j=(nonzero unit)y². At infinity put t=1/x and v=y/x³: v²=prod(1-a_j t), so a local holomorphic square root gives two unramified infinity charts. Bounded x-pieces plus the two closed infinity-chart discs cover X compactly; monodromy around any a_j exchanges the two sheets, so X is connected. Projection X->sphere has degree two, six simple ramification points, and unramified infinity. Riemann-Hurwitz gives 2g(X)-2=2(-2)+6=2, hence g=2. The compact-genus corollary gives its disc cover D. The deck action is free and properly discontinuous, hence discrete in Aut(D); a finite-order disc automorphism has an interior fixed point, so the group is torsion free. Compactness of X makes the quotient cocompact. No prior examples-page item or out-of-plan Gauss-Bonnet theorem is consumed.

items.title: Compactness and Liouville distinguish the three models
items.statement: The sphere is distinguished from the plane and disc by compactness, while the plane cannot be biholomorphic to the disc because every bounded entire function is constant.

items.proof_strategy: Check the sphere is compact and the other two are not. If a biholomorphism C->D existed it would be bounded and nonconstant, contradicting Liouville. Explain that a constant map is excluded by bijectivity and that topological equivalence of C and D alone says nothing about biholomorphism.
